title: CELPIP General Listening — Practice Test 12
instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

listeningScripts.title: Airline Baggage Delay
listeningScripts.text: Passenger: Excuse me, my baggage didn't arrive on my flight from Vancouver. Airline Agent: I'm very sorry to hear that. Let me help you file a report. What is your confirmation number? Passenger: It's VH-4829. I arrived about an hour ago on flight AC-127. Agent: Got it. Did you check your bag through to your final destination or pick it up here in Calgary? Passenger: I checked it all the way to Calgary. I have the baggage claim ticket right here. Agent: Perfect. Can I see that? The tag number is LM-58493. Your bag is a black Samsonite roller, correct? Passenger: Yes, that's right. It has a red ribbon on the handle. Agent: Great. I've found it in the system. It actually came off the plane but was misrouted to Edmonton by mistake. It's on the next flight back to Calgary, which arrives at 6:15 PM tonight. Passenger: So I'll have it this evening? Agent: Yes, we'll have it delivered to your hotel by 8 PM. Where are you staying? Passenger: The Fairmont Palliser downtown. What compensation will I get? Agent: Because the delay is less than 24 hours and the bag will be delivered today, we'll provide a $50 travel voucher for your next flight with us.

listeningScripts.title: Neighbourhood Park Chat
listeningScripts.text: David: Hey, nice day, isn't it? Rebecca: Beautiful. Perfect weather for being outside. David: Have you lived in this neighbourhood long? Rebecca: About five years now. And you? David: Just moved here last month. Rebecca: Oh nice. You picked a good time to arrive. The summer's the best season here. David: So I'm hearing. Any recommendations for places to go? Rebecca: There's a great farmer's market on Saturday mornings at the corner of Main and Oak. The coffee shop near there is amazing too. David: Sounds good. I'll have to check it out. Rebecca: You definitely should. They have the best pastries. Oh, and the park just got new playground equipment if you have kids. David: No kids yet, but that's nice to know. Do many families live here? Rebecca: Lots of young families. It's a very friendly community. David: That's what I was hoping for. I'm looking forward to exploring more.

listeningScripts.title: Public Transit New Route Announcement
listeningScripts.text: Good afternoon. Transit Authority is pleased to announce a new rapid bus route effective September 1st. The new Route 95 Express connects downtown to the northern suburbs, with stops at Central Station, City Hall, the Hospital, University Campus, and North Terminal. Service runs Monday through Friday from 6 AM to 10 PM, with departures every fifteen minutes during peak hours, 7 to 9 AM and 4 to 7 PM. Off-peak service is every thirty minutes. Weekend service begins December, with departures every twenty minutes from 9 AM to 8 PM. The Route 95 uses the new dedicated bus lane on Main Street, reducing travel time from downtown to North Terminal from forty-five minutes to approximately twenty-two minutes. Fares are the same as existing routes: single trip is three dollars fifty cents, and a monthly pass is ninety dollars. Seniors and students receive a twenty percent discount. The new buses feature USB charging ports, free Wi-Fi, and comfortable seating. Detailed schedules are available on our website and at all transit stations. Real-time tracking is available through our mobile app.

listeningScripts.title: New Tech Campus Opens in Calgary
listeningScripts.text: A major technology development is happening in Calgary today. TechHub Prairie, a 50,000-square-meter innovation center, officially opened its doors this morning in the downtown core. The facility cost 85 million dollars to construct and is expected to create 1,200 new jobs over the next two years. The campus features office space, research laboratories, and startup incubator units. Over 40 companies have already committed to moving in, including software firms, AI research groups, and digital marketing agencies. Mayor Jyoti Gondek attended the ribbon-cutting ceremony and called it a game-changer for Alberta's economy. The provincial government provided 15 million dollars in funding to support the project. TechHub Prairie will also host weekly networking events and offer mentorship programs for emerging entrepreneurs. Officials believe this development positions Calgary as a serious competitor in Canada's tech industry.

listeningScripts.title: Workplace Safety Initiative
listeningScripts.text:
Safety Officer Tom: I've been analyzing our workplace incident reports from the past two years, and I'm concerned about our trend. We've had 34 reported injuries this year, which is up 15 percent from last year. Most incidents are slips, trips, and falls in warehouse areas. I'm proposing we implement mandatory safety training for all warehouse staff every six months, not annually as we currently do.

Warehouse Manager David: Tom, I appreciate your concern, but I'm worried about requiring training every six months. That's a lot of time away from work. My team's productivity is already under pressure with current targets. If we pull people off the floor for training frequently, we'll fall further behind on our goals. Can't we just focus on better signage and equipment?

Worker Representative Angela: I actually support Tom's proposal. I work in the warehouse, and I've seen some close calls that could have been serious. The issue isn't signage—we know the hazards. The problem is we get complacent. Regular training keeps safety top of mind. Plus, Tom, I think twice-yearly training would actually improve morale because workers feel the company cares about their wellbeing.

Safety Officer Tom: Thank you, Angela. David, I understand your concern about productivity, but consider the cost of injuries. Each workplace injury costs us about $12,000 in direct and indirect costs. If we can prevent even three injuries per year, the training pays for itself. And research shows regular safety training actually reduces injuries, which ultimately improves productivity.

listeningScripts.title: Universal Basic Income Feasibility
listeningScripts.text: I want to discuss Universal Basic Income, or UBI, and why I believe it could work in Canada. The concept is straightforward: every citizen receives a regular, unconditional cash payment from the government. Now, I know people immediately worry about the cost, but let me address that. First, UBI could replace many existing welfare programs that are expensive to administer. The bureaucracy involved in means-testing and eligibility verification costs billions. UBI would be simpler and less wasteful. Second, the economic stimulus of putting money in people's hands is significant. When people have financial security, they spend more, which supports businesses and creates jobs. Third, UBI addresses real problems: poverty, economic instability, and lack of opportunity. We've seen pilot projects in Kenya, Finland, and Canada that show positive outcomes. In Kenya, UBI increased business formation by 32 percent. In Finland, participants reported better mental health and less anxiety. Some worry it will make people lazy, but that's not supported by evidence. People want purpose and contribution, not just money. What UBI does is give them the freedom to pursue education, care for family, or start businesses without desperation. The real question isn't whether we can afford UBI—it's whether we can afford not to implement it. Rising inequality and automation are creating unprecedented challenges.
